endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: (3) Exempt Review – no vote needed ALL OF THE FOLLOWING MUST BE TRUE: No patient data (or truly de-identified with minimal re-ID risk). No impact on patient care/clinical decisions. Commodity functionality (i.e., generic meeting transcription not used for clinical documentation).

endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: oversight and regulation of health care AI systems must be based on risk of harm and benefit accounting for a host of factors, including but not limited to: intended and reasonably expected use(s); evidence of safety, efficacy, and equity including addressing bias; AI system methods; level of automation; transparency; and, conditions of deployment.

endorsements.title: Embedding Internal Accountability Into Health Care Institutions for Safe, Effective, and Ethical Implementation of Artificial Intelligence Into Medical Practice: A Mayo Clinic Case Study
endorsements.quote: In accordance with The Board’s risk-based approach, these teams are provided with a fast-track recommendation from a regulatory expert without full Board review.

endorsements.title: Governing Patient-Facing AI-Generated Video in Digital Health: A Risk-and-Ethics Matrix for Deployment, Monitoring, and Change Control
endorsements.quote: Low-risk, template-based, clinician-vetted educational videos that closely follow prior approved formats may undergo an expedited review focused on dossier updates, disclosure, and any material changes, whereas novel, higher-risk, psychologically sensitive, identity-based, or publicly disseminated use cases warrant fuller panel deliberation and documentation.

endorsements.title: System-Level AI Governance in Nursing: A Practical Framework for Safe and Scalable Adoption
endorsements.quote: Higher-risk applications may require more extensive pilot testing and governance review before deployment.

evidence.title: Lessons Learned and Iterative Enhancements: A 2-Year Experience with an Established Responsible AI Framework
evidence.outcome: Median evaluation lead time before vs after three-tier risk-based review
evidence.effect: Median lead time fell to 9 weeks (tier 0) and 12 weeks (tier 2) from 20 weeks before tiering; evaluations increased 5.3-fold
evidence.quote: Tier stratification reduced median evaluation lead time to 9 weeks for tier 0 and 12 weeks for tier 2, compared to 20 weeks before implementation.

commentary.bottom_line: One uncontrolled before-and-after study at a single US health system found that three-tier risk-based review shortened median evaluation lead time from 20 weeks to 9 to 12 weeks, alongside a 5.3-fold rise in evaluations. No study has tested whether risk tiering keeps high-risk tools out of expedited review or changes patient harm.

perspectives.view: The only test is a pre-post study without a comparator, covering 64 evaluations of 55 AI solutions at one US system. Median lead time fell from 20 weeks to 9 weeks (tier 0) and 12 weeks (tier 2). Secular trends may explain part of this change. The outcome measures throughput rather than safety, so certainty is very low.

The study measured speed and volume, not misrouting. No study reports how often a tool placed on the expedited track later caused harm or needed reclassification. The risk that high-risk tools receive light review therefore remains untested. Faster review of more tools may add exposure if tier criteria are applied loosely.

Evaluations rose 5.3-fold while median lead times fell. This pattern suggests that tiering may let a committee handle more requests without a matching rise in reviewer workload. The study does not report staff hours or cost, so administrators cannot yet estimate the resources needed to run triage and separate review tracks.

Four sources endorse risk-based routing. The augmented intelligence principles state that oversight must reflect risk of harm, intended use, and level of automation. The CHAI playbooks allow an exempt tier only when a tool uses no patient data, has no clinical impact, and offers commodity functionality. These criteria rest on expert consensus and case descriptions.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares risk-tiered review with uniform full review on misclassification of tool risk, post-deployment safety events, or completion of bias assessments. No study examines whether expedited tracks omit equity or language-access checks, and none follows tools after expedited approval to see how many needed escalation.
commentary.underserved_note: The single study reports no information on Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. It remains unknown whether expedited tracks apply bias and language-access review to tools that serve these patients, so health systems serving them cannot draw on direct evidence.
